claim: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) affects roughly 1 in 3000–5000 individuals.
source: RP affects roughly 1 in 3000–5000 individuals and can be inherited as autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant (ad), or X-linked disease (Chizzolini et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chizzolini et al., 2011

claim: Mutations in rhodopsin gene (RHO) account for 25% of total autosomal dominant RP cases.
source: adRP can be caused by mutations in at least 24 different known genes (RetNet: Summaries, 2023) among which mutations in rhodopsin gene (RHO) account for 25% of total adRP cases (Meng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meng et al., 2020

claim: A mutation in the RHO gene was the first identified cause of RP due to a single-base substitution at codon 23 (P23H).
source: A mutation in the RHO gene was the first identified cause of RP due to a single-base substitution at codon 23 (P23H) leading to protein misfolding and triggering the death of the rod photoreceptors (Dryja et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dryja et al., 1990

claim: RHO is located on the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q22.1).
source: RHO is located on the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q22.1) and drives the expression of a 348 amino acid G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) with seven transmembrane domains, a luminal N terminus, and a cytoplasmic C terminus.
evidence: Statement of established genetic knowledge

claim: Rhodopsin protein (RHO) is localized in the densely packed disc membrane of the rod photoreceptor outer segments.
source: Rhodopsin protein (RHO) is localized in the densely packed disc membrane of the rod photoreceptor outer segments.
evidence: Statement of established biological knowledge

claim: Currently >150 different rhodopsin mutations have been identified.
source: Currently >150 different rhodopsin mutations have been identified, all contributing through multiple mechanisms with each having distinct consequences on the protein structure and function (Athanasiou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Athanasiou et al., 2018

claim: The patient harbors four transcriptionally active intact copies of rhodopsin.
source: We (a) show advanced retinal degeneration in a male patient (68 years of age) harboring four transcriptionally active intact copies of rhodopsin
evidence: Supported by genetic testing data presented in the manuscript

claim: The patient presented with bone spicule-like pigmentation changes, optic disc pallor, and attenuation of retinal blood vessels.
source: Complete ophthalmological examination by fundus photography and spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) revealed features of RP (Hirji, 2023) including bone spicule-like pigmentation changes, optic disc pallor, and attenuation of retinal blood vessels (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by clinical examination data and fundus photography images

claim: The patient showed outer retinal atrophy due to the loss of the photoreceptor layers, sparing the central foveal region.
source: with outer retinal atrophy due to the loss of the photoreceptor layers, sparing the central foveal region (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by SD-OCT imaging data

claim: The rearrangement consisted of a 48 kb triplicated region embedded within a 188 kb duplication.
source: The rearrangement consisted of a 48 kb triplicated region embedded within a 188 kb duplication, resulting in three apparently intact RHO genes on one chromosome and a fourth, unaltered RHO gene on the homologous chromosome.
evidence: Supported by next-generation sequencing data

claim: NGS data shows a duplication-inverted triplication-duplication event.
source: Thus, the NGS data shows a duplication-inverted triplication-duplication event, in which the triplicated segment is inverted and located between correctly oriented genomic segments (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by NGS analysis and schematic representation

claim: No other additional causative variants of inherited retinal degeneration candidate genes were identified.
source: No other additional causative variants of inherited retinal degeneration candidate genes were identified.
evidence: Supported by genetic testing results

claim: The RHO copy number variants were not detected in the unaffected daughter of the patient.
source: The RHO copy number variants were not detected in the unaffected daughter of the patient.
evidence: Supported by genetic testing of family member

claim: The pedigree data included two male family members affected with RP, indicating male-male transmission, consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance.
source: Clinically collected four-generation pedigree data of the family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) included two male family members affected with RP, indicating male-male transmission, consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance.
evidence: Supported by pedigree analysis

claim: Patient retinal organoids showed photoreceptors dysgenesis.
source: Patient retinal organoids showed photoreceptors dysgenesis, with rod photoreceptors displaying stunted outer segments with occasional elongated cilia-like projections (microscopy)
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations

claim: Patient retinal organoids showed increased RHO mRNA expression.
source: increased RHO mRNA expression (quantitative real-time PCR [qRT-PCR] and bulk RNA sequencing)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and RNA sequencing data

claim: Patient retinal organoids showed elevated levels and mislocalization of rhodopsin protein (RHO) within the cell body of rod photoreceptors.
source: and elevated levels and mislocalization of rhodopsin protein (RHO) within the cell body of rod photoreceptors (western blotting and immunohistochemistry) over the extended (300 days) culture time period when compared against control organoids.
evidence: Supported by western blotting and immunohistochemistry data

claim: PR3 treatment resulted in a partial rescue of RHO protein localization from the cell body to the inner/outer segments of rod photoreceptors in patient organoids.
source: Lastly, we utilized PR3 to target NR2E3, an upstream regulator of RHO, to alter RHO expression and observed a partial rescue of RHO protein localization from the cell body to the inner/outer segments of rod photoreceptors in patient organoids.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data after PR3 treatment

claim: RHO-CNV associated adRP develops as a result of protein overexpression, thereby overloading the photoreceptor post-translational modification machinery.
source: Taken together, this study supports the clinical data indicating that RHO-CNV associated adRPdevelops as a result of protein overexpression, thereby overloading the photoreceptor post-translational modification machinery.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and pathway analysis

claim: Transgenic mice overexpressing wild-type Rho have previously demonstrated photoreceptor degeneration.
source: Transgenic mice overexpressing wild-type Rho have previously demonstrated photoreceptor degeneration, however the precise mechanism of degeneration is still unclear (Olsson et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olsson et al., 1992

claim: The patient retinal organoids displayed short initial hair-like protrusions that did not elongate at the extended culture time of 260 and 300 days.
source: Conversely, the patient retinal organoids showed short initial hair-like protrusions that did not elongate at the extended culture time of 260 and 300 days in culture by light microscopy (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by phase contrast microscopy observations

claim: Patient organoids developed connecting cilium and inner segments similar to control organoids, but failed to extend outer segments.
source: Upon assessing the 300-day-old organoids, we observed that while the patient organoids developed connecting cilium and inner segments similar to control organoids, they failed to extend outer segments.
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data

claim: There was a significant eightfold increase in the RHO levels at D120 and D300 in the patient organoids compared to controls.
source: There was a significant eightfold increase in the RHO levels at D120 and D300 in the patient organoids compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data

claim: A significant twofold increase in rod/visual arrestin (SAG) at D300 time-point was observed in the patient organoids compared to control organoids.
source: We also observed a small twofold statistically significant increase in rod/visual arrestin (SAG) at D300 time-point in the patient organoids compared to control organoids.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data

claim: Patient retinal organoids demonstrated upregulated transcriptomic levels of RHO (~eightfold) and SAG (~fourfold) compared to control organoids.
source: Patient retinal organoids demonstrated upregulated transcriptomic levels of RHO (~eightfold) and SAG (~fourfold) compared to control organoids, comparable to the differences observed in the qRT-PCR data (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA sequencing data

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis pointed to perturbation in pathways associated with defects in glycosylation especially N-linked glycosylation as well as ER and Golgi transport.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis of significantly differentially expressed genes for cellular components category pointed to perturbation in pathways associated with defects in glycosylation especially N-linked glycosylation as well as ER and Golgi transport (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data

claim: The patient organoids had mislocalized RHO protein accumulating in the photoreceptor cell soma at all analyzed time-points (D200 and >D250).
source: Compared to the control, the patient organoids had mislocalized RHO protein accumulating in the photoreceptor cell soma, at all analyzed time-points (D200 and >D250) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining data

claim: Patient retinal organoid homogenates displayed a significant 16-fold and 9-fold higher fractions of ~40 kDa monomer and ~80 kDa dimer rhodopsin content respectively in patient organoids relative to controls.
source: Patient retinal organoid homogenates displayed a significant 16-fold and 9-fold higher fractions of ~40 kDa monomer and ~80 kDa dimer rhodopsin content respectively in patient organoids relative to controls despite loading equal amounts of protein lysates by western blot (Figure 4D–D'').
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis

claim: A significant 1.5-fold increase in ~48 kDa SAG was observed in patient organoids.
source: A significant 1.5-fold increase in ~48 kDa SAG, a rhodopsin interacting protein, was also observed (Figure 4E–E').
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis

claim: PR3 treatment led to a 4-to-30-fold decrease in RHO expression in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Following qRT-PCR analysis of PR3-treated organoids compared to vehicle-treated ones, we observed a 4-to-30-fold decrease in RHO expression in a dose-dependent manner, along with smaller decreases in other rod-specific genes including NR2E3, GNAT1, and PDE6B (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data after PR3 treatment

claim: 0.25 µM PR3 treatment led to best outer segment region localization of RHO.
source: 0.25 µM treatment lead to best outer segment region localization of RHO.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining after PR3 treatment

claim: PR3 did not have any significant effects on blue-, green- and red-cone opsin genes or protein expression.
source: We did not see any significant effects of PR3 on blue-, green- and red-cone opsin genes or protein expression for these protein or cone arrestin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and immunofluorescence data

claim: A 10–30% increase in rhodopsin expression in mice caused gradual degeneration, while a three- to fivefold increase resulted in severe and rapid photoreceptor loss.
source: A 10–30% increase in rhodopsin expression in mice caused gradual degeneration, while a three- to fivefold increase resulted in severe and rapid photoreceptor loss (Olsson et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olsson et al., 1992

claim: The retinal degeneration phenotype correlates closely to the amount of RHO overexpression.
source: More recent studies show that the retinal degeneration phenotype correlates closely to the amount of RHO overexpression (Tan et al., 2001; Wen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tan et al., 2001 and Wen et al., 2009

claim: RHO overexpression overloads the rod ER, by significantly reducing the efficiency of RHO glycosylation.
source: Based on the RNA sequencing data of our current study, it is likely that RHO overexpression overloads the rod ER, by significantly reducing the efficiency of RHO glycosylation.
evidence: Inferred from RNA sequencing pathway analysis

claim: RHO undergoes N-linked glycosylation at two distinct sites, Asn-2 and Asn-15.
source: Previous studies have shown that RHO undergoes N-linked glycosylation at two distinct sites, Asn-2 and Asn-15.
evidence: Statement based on previous studies

claim: Glycosylation is believed to be critical for protein folding through interactions with chaperones as well as for the transport of rhodopsin to the outer segments.
source: This glycosylation is believed to be critical for protein folding through interactions with chaperones as well as for the transport of rhodopsin to the outer segments.
evidence: Statement based on established biological knowledge

claim: RHO protein was found to be localized in the cell soma as well as synaptic processes and neurite extensions in RHO adRP patient samples.
source: RHO protein was found to be localized in the cell soma as well as synaptic processes and neurite extensions in RHO adRP patient samples as well as other RP patients (Li et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 1995

claim: Transgenic pigs expressing human mutant RHO (Pro347Leu) showed RHO mislocalization.
source: This was also observed in transgenic pigs expressing human mutant RHO (Pro347Leu) (Li et al., 1998) as well as Xenopus expressing Q350ter (Tam et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 1998 and Tam et al., 2006

claim: The mislocalized RHO was not degraded over extended culture time of 300 days.
source: Interestingly, the mislocalized RHO was not degraded over extended culture time of 300 days.
evidence: Observation from experimental data

claim: Transgenic Rho mutant mice such as P23H mice have demonstrated the degradation of mislocalized RHO at 3 months of age.
source: Transgenic Rho mutant mice such as P23H mice have demonstrated the degradation of mislocalized RHO at 3 months of age (Price et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price et al., 2011

claim: There have been some recent reports of progressive pericentral atrophy following RPE65 gene augmentation.
source: Although visual outcomes in most treated patients have been very encouraging with significant improvement in visual field and light sensitivity (Maguire et al., 2021), there have been some recent reports of progressive pericentral atrophy (Gange et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maguire et al., 2021 and Gange et al., 2022

claim: One potential cause of RPE atrophy following RPE65 gene augmentation could be overexpression of RPE65 in the AAV-RPE65 infected cells, due to the utilization of strong promoters such as CAG.
source: One potential cause of RPE atrophy following RPE65 gene augmentation could be overexpression of RPE65 in the AAV-RPE65 infected cells, due to the utilization of strong promoters such as CAG.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observations

claim: PR3 was shown to reduce rhodopsin expression in wild-type mice but not in rd7 mice bearing Nr2e3 mutations.
source: Additionally, PR3 was shown to reduce rhodopsin expression in wild-type mice but not in rd7 mice bearing Nr2e3 mutations.
evidence: Statement based on previous studies

claim: PR3 has been found to be safe and effective in mitigating retinal degeneration, and improving visual function in the P23H rhodopsin mouse model.
source: Upon delivery to mice by intraperitoneal injection, PR3 has been found to be safe and effective in mitigating retinal degeneration, and improving visual function in the P23H rhodopsin mouse model (Nakamura et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2017

claim: This is the first reported study of characterizing the RHO-CNV, a novel cause of adRP.
source: This is the first reported study of characterizing the RHO-CNV, a novel cause of adRP.
evidence: Statement of novelty of the study

claim: RHO expression requires precise control for rod photoreceptor functioning and maintenance.
source: Taken together, the results of this study demonstrate that RHO expression requires precise control for rod photoreceptor functioning and maintenance.

claim: The patient was 68 years of age at the time of examination.
source: We (a) show advanced retinal degeneration in a male patient (68 years of age) harboring four transcriptionally active intact copies of rhodopsin
evidence: Clinical data from patient examination

claim: Control retinal organoids displayed long hair-like protrusions which were presumptive inner and outer segments at the apical side of the retinal organoids.
source: Over the prolonged differentiation culture timeframe (>200 days), the control retinal organoids displayed long hair-like protrusions which were presumptive inner and outer segments at the apical side of the retinal organoids, a critical event indicating the start of photoreceptor maturation.
evidence: Observation from light microscopy

claim: There were no clear visible anatomical changes in apical-basal retinal cell-type distribution during the early differentiation timeframe in patient organoids.
source: Notably, there were no clear visible anatomical changes in apical-basal retinal cell-type distribution during the early differentiation timeframe, when the cone and rod photoreceptors are usually born in 45- to 50-day-old and 90- to 120-day-old human retinal organoids, respectively (data not shown).

claim: Pan-photoreceptor and early rod marker genes showed similar expression levels with no noticeable variations in RC and RM organoids.
source: Pan-photoreceptor and early rod marker genes showed similar expression levels with no noticeable variations in RC and RM organoids.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data

claim: Patient retinal organoids demonstrated increases in phototransduction cascades including the visual/light perception and membrane potential/Ca+ signaling pathways compared to control organoids.
source: Following the gene ontology enrichment analysis (EnrichGO) of significant differentially upregulated genes, we confirmed increases in phototransduction cascades including the visual/light perception and membrane potential/Ca+ signaling pathways in patient organoids compared to control organoids.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data

claim: Increases in genes associated with the synaptic signaling pathway were detected in patient organoids, suggestive of photoreceptor dysfunction.
source: Additionally, increases in genes associated with the synaptic signaling pathway were also detected, suggestive of photoreceptor dysfunction (Figure 3C).

claim: Pan-photoreceptor precursor and progenitor proteins (OTX2, CRX), and rod-specific proteins (NR2E3) were expressed in the apical layer of the organoids in a similar pattern both in the control and patient organoids.
source: Pan-photoreceptor precursor and progenitor proteins (OTX2, CRX), and rod-specific proteins (NR2E3) were expressed in the apical layer of the organoids in a similar pattern both in the control and patient organoids with equivalent photoreceptors and outer nuclear layer thickness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).

claim: The distribution of RHO protein was observed in the outer segments of control organoids starting at D200.
source: As the organoids began to mature, the distribution of RHO protein was observed in the outer segments of control organoids starting at D200, earliest time-point for detection in human retinal organoids using our differentiation protocol.
evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence staining

claim: There was no difference in apoptosis between the patient and control organoids.
source: There was also no difference in apoptosis between the patient and control organoids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL analysis

claim: The ER stress-unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway in the patient organoids did not show any differences compared to control.
source: Additionally, we analyzed the ER stress-unfolded protein response (UPR) pathway in the patient organoids and did not detect any differences compared to control (data not shown).
evidence: Experimental analysis of UPR pathway

claim: None of the PR3-treated organoids showed any evidence of toxicity by TUNEL.
source: None of the organoids showed any evidence of toxicity (by TUNEL, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) post treatment.
evidence: Supported by TUNEL analysis after PR3 treatment

claim: 0.5 µM PR3 treatment led to the strongest reduction in RHO with very few rods still expressing the protein.
source: 0.5 µM treatment led to the strongest reduction in RHO with very few rods still expressing the protein.

claim: RHO expression levels in the patient organoids treated with 0.1 and 0.25 µM PR3 were not significantly different from control organoids.
source: Upon comparison of PR3-treated patient organoids with control (RC) organoids, RHO expression levels in the patient organoids treated with 0.1 and 0.25 µM PR3 were not significantly different from control organoids.

claim: 0.5 µM PR3 resulted in significantly decreased RHO expression, much lower than the RHO levels observed in control organoids.
source: However, 0.5 µM PR3 resulted in significantly decreased RHO expression, much lower than the RHO levels observed in control organoids (Figure 5D).

claim: PR3-treated organoids were more alike to control organoids than the vehicle-treated patient organoids based on principal component analysis.
source: Principal component analysis and normalized read counts analysis of sequenced data for rod (RHO, SAG, GNAT1, NR2E3) and other genes demonstrated that the PR3-treated organoids were more alike to control organoids than the vehicle-treated patient organoids (Figure 6B and C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Several rod pathway components which were upregulated in patient organoids compared to control organoids were potentially salvaged following PR3 treatment.
source: Upon KEGG analysis of differentially expressed genes associated with the rod phototransduction pathway between the three groups of organoids, we observed that several rod pathway components which were upregulated in patient organoids compared to control organoids were potentially salvaged following PR3 treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis

claim: EnrichGO analysis of significantly upregulated genes pointed to changes in cilium organization, axoneme assembly, ER to Golgi transport, and glycosylation following PR3 treatment.
source: Analysis for significantly upregulated genes pointed to changes in cilium organization, axoneme assembly, ER to Golgi transport, and glycosylation. All of these genes are critically required for outer segment formation and protein trafficking (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C) suggestive of rod photoreceptor maturation recovery.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: PR3 could potentially rescue rod photoreceptor homeostasis in RHO-CNV patients.
source: Thus, the data presented strongly suggests that PR3 could potentially rescue rod photoreceptor homeostasis in RHO-CNV patients.

claim: PR3 confirmed the specific activity in retina based on EnrichGO analysis of significantly downregulated genes in visual perception/phototransduction pathways.
source: EnrichGO analysis of significantly downregulated genes in visual perception/phototransduction pathways confirmed the specific activity of PR3 in retina (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis

claim: PR3 did not have any adverse effects on cone opsin transcripts in patient organoids.
source: Consistent with the qRT-PCR gene expression analysis, the results showed a significant downregulation in RHO and other rod phototransduction genes including SAG and GNAT1 between the PR3 and vehicle-treated patient organoids (Figure 6A). Additionally, we confirmed that PR3 did not have any adverse effects on cone opsin transcripts in patient organoids.
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA sequencing data

claim: Careful individualized dose management of PR3 will likely be required to achieve adequate reduction of mutant rhodopsin expression in cases of adRP.
source: However, in the case of other adRP RHO mutations, careful individualized dose management of the drug will likely be required to achieve adequate reduction of mutant rhodopsin expression in cases of adRP such that it no longer causes a toxic dominant negative effect while still allowing adequate wild-type RHO expression to allow for normal rod function as complete loss of rhodopsin can cause recessive RP.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about therapeutic application
